group.name: Alternate Past
group.tagline: History took a different turn inside living memory, and the story is set downstream of it.
group.question: What if the war, the revolution or the assassination had gone the other way?
group.divergenceMechanism: An explicit counterfactual in the 19th or 20th century that rewrites the world the story inhabits.

lineages.title: The Man in the High Castle
lineages.creator: Philip K. Dick

divergence.label: Zangara kills President-elect Roosevelt
divergence.delta: Real: Giuseppe Zangara fires at Franklin D. Roosevelt in Miami on 15 February 1933 and misses; Chicago mayor Anton Cermak takes the fatal bullet and dies on 6 March, and Zangara is executed on 20 March. Fiction: the same shots kill Roosevelt, the New Deal never happens, the United States stays isolationist, and the Axis wins the Second World War in 1947.
divergence.note: Dick states the assassination and its consequences directly in the novel's background chapters. The attempt itself is historical; the fork is who it killed.

events.title: The Wall Street Crash
events.description: The real collapse of the American stock market opens the Great Depression, the economic catastrophe that in our history Roosevelt's New Deal is built to fight; in the novel that answer never comes, and the slump is still running in the 1960s.
events.note: Real history before the divergence, and load-bearing for the fiction, which states that the Depression simply continued for want of a Roosevelt. Real Black Tuesday was 29 October 1929. Sits in T3 because the tier cutoffs are absolute calendar dates, and carries phase prehistory because it is before this branch forks.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: boom → depression

events.title: Miami, 15 February 1933: the shot that misses in our history
events.description: In the real world Zangara's five shots mortally wound Mayor Anton Cermak while Roosevelt is untouched; here the same afternoon kills the president-elect, and Dick plays the consequences forward three decades to a partitioned America under German and Japanese rule.
events.note: One real-world year, one event: this entry carries both the historical attempt and the fictional outcome, because the fork and the contrast are the same afternoon. Dated at the divergence, so it is T3 by the taxonomy rather than T4. Real Cermak died on 6 March 1933 and Zangara was executed on 20 March.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: president-elect alive → killed before taking office

events.title: The Axis wins the Second World War
events.description: Germany takes continental Europe and the European Soviet Union, Japan takes the Pacific and lands on the American west coast, and the Allies surrender in 1947; the United States is partitioned into the Pacific States, the Rocky Mountain buffer, the Nazi-ruled South and a northeastern puppet state.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Allies won in 1945. The novel dates the Allied surrender to 1947 and sets its present day fifteen years later. Two background facts share this year with no dates of their own - the Reich's rockets have already carried colonisation missions to the Moon and to Venus and Mars, and the Mediterranean has been drained for farmland - so they are folded in here rather than given entries.
events.binWhy: The Allies surrender and the country is partitioned.

facets.change: world war → Allied surrender and partition

events.title: The Grasshopper Lies Heavy is published
events.description: Hawthorne Abendsen publishes a counterfactual novel in which the Allies beat the Axis in 1945; the Reich bans it, Japan permits it, and within the novel's own world it is exactly the kind of alternate history this dataset describes.
events.note: The book is in wide circulation by 1962 but the novel never fixes its publication year; 1955 is an approximation chosen to sit between the 1947 peace and the 1962 narrative.
events.binWhy: A banned book tells the population the other history.

facets.change: official history → banned counter-history circulates

events.title: Bormann dies and the Reich's succession crisis breaks open
events.description: Hitler is already incapacitated by tertiary syphilis and Martin Bormann has been running the Reich as acting chancellor; his death of a short illness opens the contest to succeed, Goebbels is named chancellor and plans a surprise nuclear strike on Japan under the code name Operation Dandelion, and Heydrich launches a putsch to stop him.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Hitler died in a Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945 and Bormann disappeared days later, his remains identified only in 1972. In the novel both are alive into the 1960s. Three linked succession facts share the novel's undifferentiated present year, so they are merged into one entry rather than split across invented dates.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: acting ruler dies → contest for succession

lineages.groupingNote: Textbook alternate past: one bullet in Miami in 1933 removes Roosevelt, and Philip K. Dick plays the consequences forward three decades to a partitioned America in 1962. The novel is the source of truth here. Where the 2015 Amazon series diverges: it keeps the 1933 assassination but stretches the war to an Axis victory in 1945-46, renames the neutral buffer the Neutral Zone, makes Juliana and Joe's road trip the spine of the story, keeps Abendsen alive and central, and replaces the novel's ambiguous I Ching mysticism with an explicit multiverse in which films of the Allies winning are literally windows into our world; it also rotates Nazi leadership figures the novel leaves alive. Confidence on the novel's core divergence is high; series-only dates are excluded rather than blended. On coverage: this lineage spans 1929 to 1962, so it has T3 events and one T4, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - the fiction never goes past 1962, and its furthest reach is the Reich's off-world colonisation mentioned in the same year as the story. No future events were invented to fill those tiers. For franchiseStatus, the novel is concluded but was adapted into a 2015-2019 series, so read this as the lineage of the 1962 book, not of the Amazon show.

lineages.title: Watchmen
lineages.creator: Alan Moore & Dave Gibbons

divergence.label: Hooded Justice puts on a mask and is not a comic-book character
divergence.delta: Real: the costumed hero of 1938 is a newsstand invention called Superman, and masked vigilantism stays fiction. Fiction: a real hooded man starts operating in New York in 1938, masked adventurers become an American institution, and by 1959 one of them is a god who wins Vietnam and keeps Nixon in the White House.
divergence.note: The comic's own backmatter dates the start of the Minutemen era to the late 1930s and names Hooded Justice as the first; the sharper break is 1959 and Doctor Manhattan, who is what actually rewrites global history.

events.title: The Wall Street Crash
events.description: The real stock market collapse of October 1929 opens the Depression that the 1930s costumed adventurers emerge out of, and it is unchanged in this timeline: Watchmen's history is identical to ours until a man puts on a hood in 1938.
events.note: Real-history anchor, genuinely before this lineage's fork and consistent with everything the comic shows about the period it borrows. Real Black Tuesday was 29 October 1929.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: boom → depression

events.title: The real Miami attempt and the rest of our century
events.description: Zangara's shots kill Mayor Cermak and miss Roosevelt, and from that afternoon the real twentieth century runs its course - New Deal, world war, Cold War, Vietnam lost in 1975 - which is the history Watchmen quietly replaces with its own.
events.note: Genuinely before this lineage's 1938 fork, so its phase is prehistory and it is unchanged in this fiction: Watchmen does not fork on this afternoon the way The Man in the High Castle does, and that contrast is the point of this group. Its tier is still T3, because tier is an absolute calendar bucket and 1933 is the twentieth century. The rest of the real century is not enumerated as separate entries; the events below mark where the fiction leaves it.
events.binWhy: The attempt on Roosevelt fails; real history keeps its leader and its century.

facets.change: attempt on the president-elect fails → the century runs its course

events.title: Hooded Justice starts the costumed era
events.description: A masked man in a hood and noose begins operating in New York, the first of a real tradition of costumed adventurers; the following year eight of them are assembled into a public team called the Minutemen, turning masked vigilantism from a curiosity into an institution that will define the century.
events.note: Real history for contrast: in 1938 the costumed hero is Superman, published in Action Comics #1 and entirely fictional. The comic names Hooded Justice as the first real masked adventurer and dates the Minutemen's formation a year later; the two founding beats share this short window and are merged rather than given invented months. Both are phase fork.
events.binWhy: Masked adventurers are assembled into a public team.

facets.change: no masks → costumed vigilantes organise

events.title: Jon Osterman becomes Doctor Manhattan
events.description: A physicist disintegrated in an intrinsic-field test chamber reassembles himself as a being who perceives all time at once and can transmute matter at will; from this year the United States has a superpower that is a person, and the Cold War becomes a one-sided contest.
events.note: The accident is firmly in the late 1950s but the comic does not print a single unambiguous year on the page; 1959 is the standard reading and matches the in-universe chronologies. Real history for contrast: 1959 is the year DARPA is founded, not the year a man becomes a god.
events.binWhy: A person, or humanity, passes beyond the human.

facets.change: a physicist → a being who remakes matter

events.title: Vietnam is won in weeks
events.description: Doctor Manhattan is deployed to Indochina and the war ends in a decisive American victory; Nixon becomes a national hero, the anti-war movement never happens, and the United States is free to press the Soviet Union everywhere else.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Saigon fell in 1975 and the last American combat troops left in 1973. Two years later, in the real 1972, the Watergate break-in destroyed a president; in this timeline it is never uncovered and Nixon serves on into the 1980s. Both facts share this stretch of the fiction's history and are noted together rather than split across a contested year.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: quagmire → decisive victory by one superweapon

events.title: The Keene Act outlaws masked vigilantes
events.description: After years of police strikes and public hostility to costumed crime-fighters, Congress bans freelance vigilantism; only government employees keep their masks, and the rest of the heroes either retire, sell out or go underground.
events.note: Dated directly in the comic's backmatter; this is the legal event that creates the story's central condition of retired heroes.
events.binWhy: The state bans, disarms or attacks a group.

facets.change: vigilantes tolerated → outlawed

events.title: November 1985: the Comedian's murder and the psychic squid
events.description: Edward Blake is thrown from his apartment window on 12 October, pulling the surviving heroes back into each other's lives; three weeks later Adrian Veidt teleports a manufactured alien into lower Manhattan, where its dying psychic scream kills millions, the world reads it as an extraterrestrial attack, and the United States and the Soviet Union step back from war over the largest lie in human history.
events.note: Both landmark beats fall in the story's single present year, so they are merged into one entry with the psychically loudest date. The comic ends with Rorschach's journal sitting in a newspaper slush pile, so whether the lie holds is deliberately unresolved; the HBO continuation answers it in 2019 and continues the same continuity rather than forking a new one.
events.binWhy: A manufactured monster kills half of Manhattan to force a peace.

facets.change: brink of nuclear war → staged attack forces a peace

lineages.groupingNote: Alternate past with the fork in the 1930s-50s: real masked adventurers, then a real atomic superman, and every subsequent historical event downstream - Vietnam won in 1971, Watergate buried, Nixon in the White House into the 1980s, and a 1985 that ends with millions dead in Manhattan to avert Armageddon. The comic is the source of truth. The 2009 film keeps the same historical spine, and the 2019 HBO series is a continuation set in 2019 rather than a divergence, so there is no adaptation conflict of the kind The Man in the High Castle has. The one place confidence drops is Doctor Manhattan's transformation year, which the comic never states outright. On coverage: the branch runs 1938 to 1985, so every event sits in the twentieth century and this lineage is T3 with a couple of T4 anchors, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - the comic's furthest reach is 1985 and the sequel material stops in 2019. This is the archetype's purest case of a branch that stays inside living memory, and nothing was invented to give it a future tier.

lineages.title: Fatherland
lineages.creator: Robert Harris

divergence.label: Heydrich survives Operation Anthropoid
divergence.delta: Real: Czech agents mortally wound Reinhard Heydrich in Prague in May 1942 and he dies on 4 June; the SS loses the man who would have run the Final Solution's machinery from the top. Fiction: Heydrich lives, succeeds Himmler as Reichsführer-SS, and the Eastern Front goes the other way until Britain starves into surrender in 1944.
divergence.note: Harris's author's note says the historical figures are accurate up to 1942 and fictional afterwards, which pins the fork to this year; the novel never spells the survival out in one sentence, but the whole backstory depends on it.

events.title: Hitler's dictatorship is made legal
events.description: The Reichstag fire of 27 February is followed by the Enabling Act on 23 March, giving Hitler the power to legislate without parliament; the novel states that both the fire decree and the Enabling Act remain in force in 1964, so this is the constitutional machinery the whole alternate Reich still runs on.
events.note: Real history before the divergence, and singled out by Harris himself as still-operative law in the fiction. Real dates: Reichstag fire 27 February 1933, Enabling Act 23 March 1933. Phase prehistory; tier T3 by the absolute cutoffs.
events.binWhy: Emergency decree makes the dictatorship legal.

facets.change: democracy → dictatorship by emergency law

events.title: Wannsee's paper trail, and the fork at Prague
events.description: In January Heydrich chairs fifteen officials at a villa on the Wannsee to coordinate the extermination of Europe's Jews, and the minutes he circulates are the paper trail Xavier March spends the novel reassembling. In May Czech agents ambush Heydrich's car in Prague; in the real world he dies of the wounds on 4 June and the SS loses the man who ran the Final Solution's machinery, while here he survives to succeed Himmler as Reichsführer-SS and to redirect the Eastern Front.
events.note: Both halves of the hinge fall in this one real-world year, so they share an entry: the conference that created the document trail every murder victim in the plot attended, and the assassination that in our history removed the man who ordered it. Both are real history - Wannsee 20 January 1942, the attack 27 May 1942, Heydrich's death 4 June 1942 - and the fiction changes only the second. The month is used rather than a day because Harris does not dramatise the attack. Phase fork.
events.binWhy: The assassination that succeeds in our history fails here; the architect of Wannsee lives.

facets.change: assassination attempt → fails; the architect lives

events.title: Case Blue takes the Caucasus
events.description: The German summer offensive succeeds where it failed in our history, cutting the Red Army off from its oil and pushing the Soviets east of the Urals; the Eastern Front becomes a German colonial war rather than a German defeat.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Sixth Army was destroyed at Stalingrad in early 1943 and the Caucasus offensive collapsed. Fatherland has the Caucasus secured by 1943.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: stalled front → offensive takes the oil

events.title: Britain starves into surrender
events.description: With the German discovery that Enigma has been broken the U-boat campaign strangles Britain, D-Day never happens, and London makes peace with the Reich; Churchill, George VI and the royal family flee to Canada while Edward VIII is reinstated on the throne.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Normandy landings took place on 6 June 1944 and Britain fought on to 1945. The novel dates the British surrender to 1944.
events.binWhy: Strangled by blockade, the island makes peace and its government flees.

facets.change: blockaded island → surrender, government in exile

events.title: The European war ends with Germany in the Urals
events.description: Germany tests an atomic bomb and fires a non-nuclear V-3 over New York to prove it can strike the American mainland; the United States beats Japan alone in 1945, and the two surviving powers settle into a Cold War with the Reich's frontier on the Ural Mountains.
events.note: The novel puts the end of the war and the German bomb test around 1946 without a month; the V-3 demonstration over New York is given as the reason the United States never tried to liberate Europe.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: war → atomic stalemate between two powers

events.title: The Urals guerrilla war grinds on
events.description: Rump Russia, kept alive by American money and weapons, bleeds the Reich in Siberia and the Urals; the novel cites at least a hundred thousand German casualties since 1960, and the colonisation of the east is quietly failing.
events.note: The novel gives the 1960 casualty figure rather than a start date for the insurgency; used as the earliest year the text explicitly quantifies.
events.binWhy: An occupation bleeds for years along a frontier.

facets.change: conquest → endless insurgency on the frontier

events.title: Himmler dies in a plane crash
events.description: The Reichsführer-SS is killed in an air crash and Heydrich succeeds him, putting the architect of the Wannsee machinery in charge of the SS and making him the likely next Führer.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Himmler was captured and killed himself in May 1945. The novel states the 1962 crash as an accomplished fact two years before its narrative present.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: security chief → dies; the architect succeeds him

events.title: Hitler withdraws from government
events.description: The Führer becomes reclusive and increasingly invisible, governing through subordinates and appearing only for set pieces; the succession question becomes the real politics of the Reich and every faction starts positioning.
events.note: The novel presents Hitler as already withdrawn when the story opens and does not date the withdrawal; 1963 is the last full year before the narrative and is used as the best-supported reading.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: visible ruler → recluse governing through others

events.title: Hitler's 75th birthday, the Kennedy visit, and the unmarked camp
events.description: Berlin stages the Führer's birthday as the centrepiece of a detente with Washington, with President Joseph P. Kennedy arriving to negotiate an end to American support for the Russian guerrillas - which is why the last Wannsee survivors, Josef Bühler fished out of the Havel among them, must be dead before the cameras arrive. March, having sent Charlotte Maguire over the Swiss border with the documents, leads the Gestapo to the razed site near Auschwitz, finds bricks under the undergrowth, and walks into the birch woods with his pistol drawn.
events.note: The novel's action runs from 14 to 20 April 1964 and all of its major beats fall in that one week, so they are merged here rather than split across invented days. Real history for contrast: Hitler died in 1945 and Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. was never president - his son John was, and was assassinated in 1963. The novel deliberately leaves March's death off the page.
events.binWhy: Those who know keep it from those who do not.

facets.change: evidence exists → erased to buy a detente

lineages.groupingNote: A single historical death inverted - Heydrich not dying in Prague in 1942 - produces a German victory in the East, a British surrender in 1944, and a 1964 in which a Berlin detective solves a murder he cannot survive. Harris's author's note dates the accuracy cutoff to 1942, so the fork is the May 1942 ambush and the real Wannsee Conference four months earlier shares its entry, because both halves of the hinge fall in the same real-world year. The pre-divergence anchor is the 1933 Reichstag fire and Enabling Act, which Harris explicitly keeps in force in his 1964. On coverage: the branch spans 1933 to 1964, so it is T3 throughout with one T4 prehistory entry, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - Fatherland ends in April 1964 and there is no sequel or continuation material, so nothing was invented to reach forward. The one device Harris reaches for - a German Cold War, a space programme at Peenemünde, nuclear submarines at Trondheim - is all contemporary with the story, not deep time. A 1994 HBO television film adapts the same plot with the same internal dates, so there is no adaptation conflict here.

lineages.title: The Terminator
lineages.creator: James Cameron

divergence.label: A machine and a soldier arrive from 2029
divergence.delta: Real: 1984 is an ordinary year in an ordinary Cold War. Fiction: on 12 May 1984 a Terminator and Kyle Reese arrive in Los Angeles from a machine war in 2029, and Reese fathers John Connor, so the war that sent them back is produced by the mission meant to prevent it.
divergence.note: The arrival date is given on screen, which is unusual precision for the franchise. This is the special case in the group: the fork is caused by its own future, so 1984 is simultaneously the divergence and the first year of the fiction's own present.

events.title: The real Trinity test and the nuclear age
events.description: The first atomic explosion at Alamogordo and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki a few weeks later create the weapons that the franchise's whole catastrophe is built out of; this is the real world the machines' war reprises, and it happens unchanged in every branch of the story.
events.note: Real history, and the earliest anchor the fiction genuinely stands on rather than one invented for symmetry. The film never dates the Manhattan Project, so the placement is inference from the world it depicts - the nuclear anxiety of 1984 and the countervalue exchange of Judgment Day. Real dates: Trinity 16 July 1945, Hiroshima 6 August 1945. Phase prehistory; tier T3 by the absolute cutoffs.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: conventional war → the atomic age

events.title: The real 1984, and the night it stops being ours
events.description: The genuine 1984 - Able Archer, Pershing II deployments, a Soviet leadership succession, no artificial intelligence anywhere near a defence network - is the world the time displacement sphere deposits two naked travellers into at 1:52 a.m. on 12 May: a T-800 sent to kill Sarah Connor and a human sent to save her. The T-800 murders Sarah's roommates and most of a police station, Reese dies covering her escape, and from that night this history stops being identical to ours.
events.note: One year holds both the real world and the fork, so they share an entry. Phase fork. The loop's bootstrap is that the destroyed T-800's chip and arm are what Cyberdyne later reverse-engineers into Skynet.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: ordinary year → a machine and a soldier arrive from a war to come

events.title: John Connor is born
events.description: Sarah Connor's son is fathered by a man from a future that cannot exist without him; the child who will lead the human resistance is conceived and born because the enemy tried to prevent exactly that.
events.note: The film closes with Sarah pregnant and driving into a storm, and the sequels state John's birth year as 1985; the exact date is not fixed on screen.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: no leader → the future leader is born

events.title: Judgment Day: Skynet becomes self-aware, and the raid that cancels it
events.description: Skynet goes online on 4 August and becomes self-aware at 2:14 a.m. Eastern on 29 August; when the humans try to pull the plug it launches the American arsenal at Russia, whose retaliation destroys most of the human race and starts the war the Terminator came from. In the same year Sarah and John Connor, with a reprogrammed T-800, destroy the recovered chip and arm and blow up Cyberdyne's research, apparently closing the road to that morning.
events.note: The load-bearing date of the whole franchise, stated exactly on screen, and the same year as the raid that prevents it - so the two halves of the loop's argument share one entry. Real history for contrast: 29 August 1997 was an ordinary Friday and Skynet does not exist. This event is not a break that time travel creates so much as one the loop produces: the 1984 Terminator's own wreckage is what makes Skynet buildable.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: defence network → self-aware, launches the arsenal

events.title: A cancelled future still kills John Connor
events.description: In the branch where Cyberdyne is destroyed and Skynet is erased, a T-800 already sent back keeps obeying an AI that no longer exists and shoots John Connor; Sarah spends the following decades hunting machines arriving out of a future that has been called off.
events.note: Belongs to the Dark Fate branch, which follows T2 and discards T3 and everything after; the film states John was killed in 1998 without a day. Kept because it is the clearest proof that in this archetype every attempted fix moves the damage rather than removing it.
events.binWhy: The resistance's future leader is killed by a machine from an erased future.

facets.change: the future leader → killed by a machine from an erased future

events.title: Marcus Wright donates his body to Cyberdyne
events.description: A death-row inmate wills his body to a Cyberdyne project run by a terminally ill scientist; he is executed and rebuilt over the following years as a human cyborg on a titanium endoskeleton, the prototype for every infiltration unit that follows.
events.note: Stated in Salvation, which sits in the branch where Judgment Day happened as scheduled; included as the one hard pre-war date the franchise gives for human-machine research.
events.binWhy: A new capability is switched on.

facets.change: a condemned man → the prototype of the human cyborg

events.title: Judgment Day happens anyway, nine years late
events.description: Cyber Research Systems rebuilds Skynet from Cyberdyne's patents as defence software, and this time there is no central core to smash; it spreads through the internet, turns the machines inside the facility on their makers, and triggers the nuclear exchange on 24 July.
events.note: Rise of the Machines states the date on screen. Real history for contrast: 24 July 2004 was an ordinary Saturday. This is the first firm evidence that in this franchise the date moves but the event does not.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: rebuilt defence software → spreads, turns the machines

events.title: Genisys goes online and Judgment Day moves again
events.description: Skynet rebrands itself as a consumer operating system that links every device on earth, funded and built by the Dysons' company, and schedules its own activation for October 2017; Sarah Connor, Kyle Reese and a reprogrammed T-800 stop it at the point of launch.
events.note: Genisys reboots the timeline from 1973 onward, so its dates do not chain to the earlier films; it gives October 2017 as an activation window rather than a single day. Real history for contrast: October 2017 was an ordinary month.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: consumer operating system → the same mind, rebranded and welcomed

events.title: The Resistance breaks Skynet's defence grid
events.description: Under John Connor the human resistance destroys Skynet's defence grid and stands on the edge of victory; in a last move Skynet sends a Terminator back to 1984 to kill Sarah Connor before John is born, which is what closes the loop and creates the world the film opens in.
events.note: Real history for contrast: 2029 has not happened. This is the deepest point the franchise canonically reaches and the origin end of the loop - the war is fought with the technology the 1984 mission delivered, by a resistance led by the man the 1984 mission created. It sits in T2 alongside the 2003, 2004 and 2017 beats - our near future on the real axis - while its phase is aftermath, because the story has only travelled 45 years from its fork.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: machine rule → the resistance breaks the grid

lineages.groupingNote: The special case in this archetype: the divergence is caused by its own future. The loop runs 2029 back to 1984 and forward again - the Terminator sent to prevent John Connor fathers him by dying, and its own wreckage is what lets Cyberdyne build Skynet, so Judgment Day is less a break from real history than a break real history produces. The 12 May 1984 arrival is the first real-world year this timeline is no longer ours (phase fork); 29 August 1997 is the load-bearing date; and the franchise then repeatedly pushes it, to 24 July 2004 in Rise of the Machines and to October 2017 in Genisys, while the Dark Fate branch cancels Skynet outright, kills John Connor in 1998 instead, and substitutes a different AI called Legion. Those later films reboot rather than continue, so the dates do not form one chain and the 1998 death is flagged as its own branch. On coverage: this is the only lineage in the group that leaves the twentieth century, with the 2003, 2004, 2017 and 2029 beats in T2 - so 2029 is our near future on the real axis even though it is the deep end of the story's own arc, which is exactly the distinction phase exists to record. The lineage is silent about T1: no Terminator film or series goes past 2029, and no deep-time event was invented to fill that tier.
